subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 3 of Year 2 Computing at Ehel Academy. This unit is about computers and the jobs they do. There is no coding in this unit — it is all about noticing computers around us and learning the words to talk about them.

A tablet with a story app, a phone to video-call grandmother, the laptop at Ehel Academy, a smartwatch on a wrist — these are all computers. This unit helps you notice that, and gives you simple words for the parts and the jobs.

Every computer is made of two things: hardware (the parts we can touch) and software (the instructions inside, which we cannot touch).
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 2 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Name some computers (digital devices): tablet, phone, laptop, desktop, smartwatch.
Say that every computer is made of hardware and software.
Point to hardware (the parts we can touch) and give a few examples.
Say that software is the instructions inside, and that an app is software that does a job.
Say the difference between an input device (puts things in) and an output device (gets things out).
Say one or two things that make a device easy to use (user-friendly), such as being portable or having a touchscreen.

concepts.title: Computers come in many shapes
concepts.explanation:
A computer is a machine that follows instructions to do jobs for us. Computers come in many shapes and sizes. A tablet, a phone, a laptop, a big desktop, and even a smartwatch are all computers. Another name for them is digital devices.

Did you know a phone is a kind of computer? So is this tablet. And so is the laptop at Ehel Academy.
concepts.example: They come in different sizes, but they are all computers. Guide you to answers like: video-call grandmother, open a drawing app, take photos of the family, watch a story, play a counting game.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that a small phone is a computer too, not only the big desktop? Can you point to two or three computers and say one job each does?

concepts.title: Hardware: the parts we can touch
concepts.explanation:
Every computer is made of hardware. Hardware is all the parts we can see and touch — the screen, the keyboard, the mouse, the headphones. Some hardware is hidden inside where we cannot see it, but it is still there.

Touch it. The glass screen, the buttons, the case — all the parts your fingers can feel — that is the hardware.
concepts.example: If I can touch it, it is hardware. Put a tablet in a child's hands.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand the rule “hardware is what I can touch”? Can you name the screen, the keyboard and the mouse?

concepts.title: Software: the instructions inside
concepts.explanation:
A computer also needs software. Software is the set of instructions that tells the hardware what to do. We cannot touch software. An app is software that does one job — a drawing app, a story app, a counting game. Hardware and software work together: the hardware is the parts, and the software tells the parts what to do.

Your hands are a bit like hardware — they can do things. But your hands wait for your head to tell you what to do. Software is like those instructions.
concepts.example: When Leila taps the story app, the app is the software. It tells the tablet — the hardware — to show the page and play the story.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you sort a keyboard (hardware) from a game app (software)?

concepts.title: Putting things IN and getting things OUT
concepts.explanation:
Hardware can do two different jobs. Some hardware lets us put things INTO the computer — we call these input devices (a keyboard, a mouse, a microphone, a camera). Some hardware lets the computer give things OUT for us to see or hear — these are output devices (a screen, a speaker, headphones, a printer).

For input, push your hands towards yourself ("IN “). For output, push your hands away (” OUT “). Say:” When Sami types on the keyboard, he is putting letters IN. The keyboard is an input device.
concepts.example: When the printer prints his picture, the computer is giving it OUT. The printer is an output device."
concepts.checkYourself: Can you use the IN and OUT hand actions? Can you know a keyboard puts things in and a speaker gives sound out? Can you sort four devices into input and output?

concepts.title: Easy-to-use computers
concepts.explanation:
Some computers are made to be easy to use. When something is easy to use, we say it is user-friendly. A few things make a device easy to use: it is portable (small and light, so we can carry it), it is wireless (no wires to trip over), it has a big screen (easy to see), or it has a touchscreen (you just touch it).

Compare two things. Which one can you carry to the next room easily? Look, no wire! We say it is wireless. Wires can get in a tangle, so no wire is easier.
concepts.example: Point to a big, heavy desktop computer (or a picture of one) and then to a light tablet. Then show wireless headphones (or describe them) next to headphones with a wire.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you use a word like portable, wireless or touchscreen? Can you give one reason a tablet is easy to use?

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.
